title: Severe bleeding (Stop the Bleed)
summary: Call 911, press hard on the wound, pack it if it is deep, and use a tourniquet on an arm or leg that will not stop bleeding.

sources.title: DHS / Stop the Bleed - Applying a Tourniquet

blocks.text: **Call 911 or have someone call right now.** Severe bleeding can kill within minutes. Act first, then keep going until responders take over.

Stop the Bleed teaches three ways to control severe bleeding: **pressure, packing, and a tourniquet**. A class is the best way to learn them. The course takes about an hour (a 25-minute online version covers the lecture).

items: Make sure the scene is safe. Expose the wound.
Press straight down hard with a clean cloth, bandage, piece of clothing or your hand. Use both hands if you can.
Keep pressing until the bleeding stops or help takes over.
If blood soaks through, leave the first cloth in place and add more on top. Do not peek.
Once it stops, wrap the dressing firmly with tape or clean cloth.

blocks.text: For a deep wound, ACS teaches packing the wound with gauze or clothing and then pressing on it. Packing is best learned in a class. Do not pull out a knife, stick or other object that is stuck in the wound. Leave it in place.
Use one if firm pressure does not stop the bleeding and the dressing is soaked. A tourniquet is for life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg.

blocks.alt: Where a tourniquet goes on an arm or leg. Put it between the wound and the heart, at least 2 to 3 inches from the wound, and it can go over clothing. If you cannot judge that spot, FEMA says to put it as high up the limb as possible, close to the torso. Do not put it over a joint such as the elbow, knee, wrist or ankle; if a joint is in the way, go above it, toward the body. Pull the strap tight, twist the rod until the bleeding stops or slows a lot, and lock it. Write down the time, and do not loosen it. The drawing is not to scale.
blocks.caption: Where the tourniquet goes.

items: Place the tourniquet **between the wound and the heart**, at least **2 to 3 inches** from the wound. It can go over clothing.
Do **not** put it over a joint such as the elbow, knee, wrist or ankle. If a joint is in the way, go above it, toward the body.
Clip or buckle it and pull the strap as tight as you can.
Twist the windlass rod until the bleeding stops or slows a lot. This may be painful.
Lock the rod in its clip, and use the Velcro strap if there is one.
If it is still bleeding, put a second tourniquet next to or just above the first.
**Write down the time** you put it on, and tell the responders.
Leave it on until EMS takes over. Do not loosen it yourself.

blocks.text: FEMA's handout says to put the tourniquet as high up the limb as possible, close to the torso, if you cannot judge the 2-to-3-inch spot. A tourniquet left on too long can injure tissue, which is why the time matters.

If you have no tourniquet, MedlinePlus describes an improvised one made from a bandage 2 to 4 inches wide, wrapped around the limb several times and tied in a knot with a stick placed between the knots and twisted until bleeding stops. Training and a real tourniquet are far better.

items: Signs: pale, cool, clammy skin, a fast weak pulse, dizziness, confusion, weakness.
If there is no head, neck, back or leg injury, lay the person flat and raise the feet about 12 inches (30 cm).
Keep the injured part still and cover the person with a coat or blanket.
Do not give them anything to eat or drink.

blocks.text: Do not clean a large wound, probe it, or pull out anything embedded in it. Do not remove a soaked dressing. Add more on top.
